blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — healthcare fire response, compartmentation, defend-in-place, and targeted relocation
stem: A fire alarm activates on an inpatient unit after smoke is reported in one patient room. Fire doors and suppression systems are functioning. Which response best reflects healthcare fire-safety principles?

options.A: Follow the facility fire-response plan; keep patients in protected compartments when safe, and relocate occupants from threatened areas as conditions require.
options.B: Begin unit-wide vertical evacuation toward the building exit before using smoke compartments, so every patient is moved before conditions can worsen.
options.C: Keep patients in their current rooms while suppression systems operate, and wait for fire-department direction before relocating anyone from the affected area.
options.D: Move patients into the corridor nearest the exits and hold fire doors open during relocation so staff can observe conditions across the unit.

rationale: A is correct. Current Joint Commission fire-protection guidance states that healthcare occupancies are designed around compartmentation and a defend-in-place strategy rather than immediate evacuation. The organization must have and exercise a specific fire-response plan. Protected smoke compartments allow patients to remain in safe care areas, while occupants can be moved horizontally out of an unsafe environment as conditions require; total building evacuation is uncommon but remains possible when conditions demand it. B is incorrect because automatic unit-wide or building evacuation bypasses the healthcare defend-in-place/compartmentation strategy and may expose patients unnecessarily. C is incorrect because defend-in-place does not mean leaving threatened occupants in place until the fire department arrives; compartmentation also supports relocation to a safer compartment. D is incorrect because fire and smoke doors are part of the compartmentation system and Joint Commission guidance specifically emphasizes not blocking or compromising fire doors.
educational_objective: Apply healthcare fire-response principles by following the facility plan, using compartmentation to defend patients in protected areas, and relocating threatened occupants rather than defaulting to immediate total evacuation.
source_organization: The Joint Commission; National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
source_document_title: Fire Protection - EC.02.03.05; General Requirements - LS.02.01.10; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: Current Joint Commission Environment of Care/Fire Protection guidance rechecked 2026-08-20; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective April 2026
source_locator: Joint Commission Fire Protection, Clinical Impact lines 104-108: healthcare settings do not evacuate immediately; staff defend in place, the organization must have a specific fire-response plan, and staff implement that plan when alarms activate. Building Compartmentation Discussion lines 121-138: healthcare occupancies are designed to defend in place; smoke compartments support horizontal movement to a safer area; total building evacuation is rare but remains possible. Joint Commission General Requirements, Building Compartmentation: barriers protect patients while they remain in care environments, horizontal/compartment relocation is used when needed, evacuation is a last resort, and clinical staff should not block fire doors open or compromise closing/latching devices. NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan Safety and Infection Prevention and Control supports protecting clients/personnel from environmental hazards and responding to safety events according to policy.

correction_summary: Original Q0065 used absolute-word distractors and made incorrect choices easy to reject. The item was rebuilt so all four options are plausible fire-response strategies. The key requires understanding healthcare compartmentation and defend-in-place while preserving targeted relocation and facility-plan activation, rather than memorizing a universal acronym or assuming immediate total evacuation. Independent post-fetch reread found no unresolved source, fire-compartmentation, relocation, door/barrier, ambiguity, cueing, blueprint, or second-answer conflict.

option_audit.A: Correct; integrates the facility fire-response plan, defend-in-place for protected occupants, and relocation of threatened occupants as conditions require.
option_audit.B: Plausible evacuation-first approach; incorrect because healthcare occupancies are designed to use compartmentation/defend-in-place rather than default to immediate unit-wide vertical evacuation.
option_audit.C: Plausible overinterpretation of defend-in-place; incorrect because threatened occupants may need relocation to another compartment before fire-department arrival according to the facility response plan.
option_audit.D: Plausible visibility/access strategy; incorrect because holding fire doors open compromises barriers used to contain smoke/fire and conflicts with Joint Commission barrier-management guidance.

cueing_audit.absolute_words: No option relies on all/only/always/never/must-type absolute wording.
cueing_audit.answer_length: Final option lengths: A 158, B 149, C 159, D 141 characters; the key is not uniquely longest and choices are substantially balanced.
cueing_audit.grammatical_lexical: All four options describe realistic operational responses and differ in evacuation timing, compartment use, or barrier management rather than obvious tone.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: Independent adversarial reread found no defensible second answer. B bypasses defend-in-place, C prevents needed targeted relocation, and D compromises fire-door compartmentation; A is uniquely best.
